stem: A 78-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to a 3-day history of intermittent but progressive substernal chest pain. Medical history includes hypertension and hyperlipidemia, but the patient has had poor adherence with her medication and outpatient follow-up. She has a 30 pack-year smoking history. On admission, ECG reveals normal sinus rhythm with ST-segment elevation and pathologic Q waves in leads I, aVL, and V2 to V5. The patient refuses percutaneous coronary intervention and is treated medically. On the fifth day of hospitalization, she experiences severe dyspnea, sweating, and hypotension. Physical examination shows raised jugular venous pressure, no heart murmurs, and clear lungs. She rapidly loses consciousness and becomes pulseless, and the subsequent resuscitation attempt is ineffective. Which of the following most likely contributed to this patient's death?

options.A: Blood accumulation in the pericardial space
options.B: Complete rupture of the papillary muscle
options.C: Rapid reperfusion of the ischemic myocardium
options.E: True aneurysm of the ventricular wall

explanations.A: Left ventricular free wall rupture typically occurs within 5 days to 2 weeks post-transmural myocardial infarction, particularly in patients who received delayed or no reperfusion. Weakening by coagulative necrosis, macrophage infiltration, and enzymatic lysis leads to rupture, abrupt hemopericardium, and acute cardiac tamponade (blood accumulation in pericardial space) with obstructive shock and PEA cardiac arrest.
explanations.B: Papillary muscle rupture presents with acute severe mitral regurgitation, a new holosystolic murmur, and marked pulmonary edema with bilateral crackles.
explanations.C: Reperfusion injury can precipitate lethal arrhythmias but requires acute mechanical or pharmacological reperfusion, which this patient refused.
explanations.D: Interventricular septal rupture results in a left-to-right shunt, manifesting as a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border and biventricular failure with pulmonary edema.
explanations.E: A true left ventricular aneurysm develops weeks to months after MI and presents with subacute heart failure or persistent ST elevation rather than acute hemopericardium.

generalExplanation: This patient suffered an extensive transmural anterior MI and experienced sudden death on day 5 with signs of acute cardiac tamponade (hypotension, elevated JVP, clear lungs, pulseless electrical activity). Left ventricular free wall rupture is a mechanical complication of transmural MI occurring between days 3 and 14 (peak days 4–7), when coagulative necrosis and macrophage-mediated enzymatic degradation leave the myocardial wall at its weakest point.
educationalObjective: Left ventricular free wall rupture is a mechanical complication occurring up to 2 weeks after transmural myocardial infarction. Rapid blood extravasation into the pericardial sac produces acute cardiac tamponade and obstructive shock.

stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to increasing dyspnea. He was unable to mow his lawn the previous day due to shortness of breath. The patient has a history of hypertension and a 20-pack-year smoking history. He is retired and traveled to Hawaii 2 months ago. Blood pressure is 160/86 mm Hg, pulse is 94/min, and respirations are 24/min; oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. Physical examination reveals bilateral lung crackles and occasional wheezes. Laboratory testing reveals elevated brain natriuretic peptide levels. Which of the following is the primary trigger for the release of this substance in this patient?

options.C: Decrease in vena cava blood return

explanations.A: Juxtacapillary (J) receptors in alveolar walls are stimulated by interstitial pulmonary edema and increase the respiratory rate (tachypnea), but do not trigger BNP synthesis.
explanations.B: Decreased renal perfusion pressure stimulates renin secretion by juxtaglomerular cells, activating the RAAS cascade to promote vasoconstriction and sodium retention (counteracting natriuretic peptides).
explanations.C: Decreased vena cava return reduces preload, which would decrease (not increase) natriuretic peptide release.
explanations.D: Myocardial necrosis releases cardiac troponins and CK-MB into the blood.
explanations.E: Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) is synthesized and released primarily by ventricular cardiomyocytes in response to increased ventricular wall stress, stretch, and volume overload. BNP induces systemic vasodilation and natriuresis/diuresis to attenuate hemodynamic strain on the failing heart.
explanations.F: Stretching of aortic and carotid baroreceptors modulates autonomic output via cranial nerves IX and X to decrease sympathetic discharge, but does not secrete BNP.

generalExplanation: In patients with congestive heart failure, elevated left ventricular end-diastolic volume and pressure increase myocardial wall tension (wall stress = Pressure × Radius / (2 × Thickness), according to Laplace's law). Increased ventricular wall stretch triggers release of pre-pro-BNP from ventricular myocytes, which is cleaved into active BNP and inactive NT-proBNP. Both ANP (from atria) and BNP (from ventricles) stimulate membrane-bound guanylate cyclase, increasing intracellular cGMP to promote arterial and venous vasodilation and renal natriuresis.
educationalObjective: The ventricular myocardium secretes brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) in response to the ventricular stretch and strain that typically occurs with volume overload. BNP, along with atrial natriuretic peptide secreted by the atrial myocardium, stimulates vasodilation and salt and water excretion to help relieve volume overload.

stem: A 77-year-old man comes to the office after he was found to have high blood pressure during a health fair. The patient denies any medical problems and feels proud that he has not needed to see a doctor for many years. His blood pressure is 170/70 mm Hg and pulse is 74/min. Other physical examination findings are normal. The patient is started on a medication to treat his hypertension. During his follow-up visit 3 weeks later, he reports bilateral leg swelling. He has no chest pain, shortness of breath, or abdominal symptoms. His blood pressure is 135/65 mm Hg and pulse is 80/min. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal, but there is bilateral, symmetrical, 2+ pitting lower extremity edema. Laboratory studies show serum creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL, and urinalysis is negative for proteinuria. Which of the following was most likely prescribed to treat this patient's hypertension?

explanations.A: Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that selectively dilates precapillary arterioles. This preferentially increases intracapillary hydrostatic pressure, causing transudation of fluid into the interstitial space and resulting in dependent, bilateral peripheral edema.
explanations.B: Eplerenone is a selective aldosterone antagonist that promotes natriuresis and can cause hyperkalemia, but does not cause peripheral edema.
explanations.C: Hydrochlorothiazide causes volume depletion, hypokalemia, and hyperuricemia, rather than dependent edema.
explanations.D: Ramipril causes postcapillary venodilation, which actually reduces capillary hydrostatic pressure and helps relieve or prevent calcium channel blocker-induced peripheral edema.
explanations.E: Torsemide is a loop diuretic used to reduce fluid volume and treat edema.
explanations.F: Valsartan, an ARB, dilates postcapillary venules and reduces precapillary filtration pressure.

generalExplanation: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (eg, amlodipine, nifedipine) reduce systemic vascular resistance by blocking L-type calcium channels on vascular smooth muscle. However, their vasodilatory effect is selective for precapillary arterioles rather than postcapillary venules. The resulting unbalanced arteriolar dilation increases capillary hydrostatic pressure, driving fluid extravasation into dependent soft tissues to cause peripheral edema. Co-administration of an ACE inhibitor or ARB causes balanced postcapillary venodilation, normalizing capillary hydrostatic pressure and reducing CCB-induced edema.
educationalObjective: Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker commonly used as monotherapy or in combination with other agents for treatment of hypertension. Major side effects include headache, flushing, dizziness, and peripheral edema.

stem:
An 8-hour-old boy is being assessed for a murmur in the newborn nursery. The patient was born at 37 weeks via cesarean delivery. Apgar scores were 7 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. He was noted to have a harsh ejection systolic murmur of 4/6 intensity during initial newborn examination. Brachial and femoral pulses are 2+ with no delay. While the patient is breastfeeding for the first time, his face, lips, hands, and feet become cyanotic. The murmur cannot be heard during the cyanotic episode. Which of the following oxygen saturation percentages are most likely present during the cyanotic episode?

| Options | Right atrium | Right ventricle | Pulmonary artery | Pulmonary veins | Left atrium | Left ventricle |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| A. | 75 | 75 | 75 | 98 | 98 | 80 |
| B. | 75 | 75 | 75 | 98 | 80 | 80 |
| C. | 75 | 85 | 85 | 98 | 98 | 98 |
| D. | 80 | 80 | 80 | 98 | 98 | 98 |
| E. | 75 | 75 | 80 | 98 | 98 | 98 |

explanations.A: The infant has Tetralogy of Fallot (ToF). During feeding/crying, acute spasm of the infundibular septum increases RVOT obstruction, shutting off flow across the pulmonic valve (causing the systolic murmur to disappear). Deoxygenated blood from the RV (75% O2) is forced right-to-left across the VSD directly into the left ventricle, mixing with pulmonary venous return (98% O2) to lower LV saturation to ~80% and cause systemic cyanosis. Left atrial saturation remains normally oxygenated at 98%.
explanations.B: A step-down in left atrial saturation indicates right-to-left shunting at the atrial level (eg, via ASD/PFO in Eisenmenger syndrome or tricuspid atresia).
explanations.C: Step-up in saturation from RA (75%) to RV (85%) reflects left-to-right shunting through a VSD during acyanotic resting periods in ToF.
explanations.D: Represents normal cardiac chamber oxygen saturation distribution without shunts.
explanations.E: Step-up in saturation at the pulmonary artery level (80%) reflects left-to-right shunting across a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

generalExplanation: In Tetralogy of Fallot, dynamic infundibular spasm during periods of agitation, crying, or feeding increases resistance through the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT). This reduces blood flow through the pulmonary valve—making the harsh systolic ejection murmur disappear—and diverts desaturated blood right-to-left across the VSD into the overriding aorta and left ventricle. The resulting decrease in left ventricular and systemic arterial oxygen saturation (~80%) produces the classic hypercyanotic 'tet spell'.
educationalObjective: Tetralogy of Fallot involves right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction and a ventricular septal defect (VSD). Cyanotic ('tet') episodes are commonly precipitated by a dynamic increase in RVOT obstruction that increases right-to-left shunting through the VSD. These episodes involve decreased blood flow through the RVOT, causing disappearance of the associated systolic murmur, and reduced oxygen saturation of the left ventricular blood being pumped into the systemic circulation.

stem:
Researchers conduct an experiment to determine hemodynamic changes during exercise. Invasive monitoring of various parameters is performed to obtain a left ventricular pressure-volume loop. Compared to at rest, which of the following changes is most likely to be observed during moderate to heavy exercise? (solid line: at rest; dashed line: during exercise)

- Option A: PV loop showing increased end-diastolic volume (preload), shifted leftward end-systolic volume (increased inotropic contractility), increased peak systolic pressure (afterload), and widened horizontal width (increased stroke volume)
- Option B: PV loop showing increased contractility without increased preload
- Option C: PV loop showing increased afterload with decreased stroke volume (aortic stenosis pattern)
- Option D: PV loop showing increased preload with no increase in contractility (saline infusion pattern)
- Option E: PV loop showing decreased preload and decreased stroke volume (nitroglycerin pattern)

options.A: Loop A (Increased preload, increased contractility, increased afterload, increased stroke volume)
options.C: Loop C (Increased afterload, decreased stroke volume)
options.E: Loop E (Decreased preload and decreased stroke volume)

explanations.A: During moderate to heavy exercise, sympathetic-mediated venoconstriction mobilizes venous reservoir blood, increasing venous return and LV end-diastolic volume (increased preload). Sympathetic inotropic stimulation increases contractility (shifting the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship up and to the left). Both factors dramatically increase stroke volume. Despite vasodilation in exercising muscle decreasing total SVR, the large surge in stroke volume and inotropy drives peak systolic aortic and LV pressure higher, producing an overall increase in peak LV afterload.
explanations.B: Isolated increased contractility without increased preload describes inotropic drug administration (eg, digoxin, dobutamine).
explanations.C: Increased afterload with decreased stroke volume reflects fixed LV outflow tract obstruction (eg, aortic stenosis).
explanations.D: Increased preload with unchanged contractility describes passive intravascular volume expansion with isotonic saline.
explanations.E: Decreased preload with decreased stroke volume and decreased afterload describes pure venodilator therapy (eg, sublingual nitroglycerin).

generalExplanation:
Hemodynamic adaptations during aerobic exercise:
1. Preload: Venoconstriction and muscle pump increase venous return, expanding LVEDV (shifting right border rightward).
2. Contractility: Sympathetic beta-1 activation increases myocardial inotropy, reducing LVESV (shifting left border leftward).
3. Stroke Volume: The combination of increased preload and decreased end-systolic volume widens the PV loop horizontally.
4. Afterload: Although systemic arteriolar resistance in working muscle decreases, the massive increase in stroke volume and ejection force raises peak systolic arterial pressure (shifting upper border upward).
educationalObjective: With moderate to heavy exercise, the changes to the left ventricular pressure-volume loop include increased preload and increased contractility that both contribute to increased stroke volume. Although reduced systemic vascular resistance decreases afterload, the increase in systolic pressure caused by increased preload and contractility override the decrease, resulting in overall increased afterload.

stem: A 54-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to severe shortness of breath and palpitations. During initial assessment, pulse oximetry shows 83%. Diffuse, bilateral crackles are heard on lung auscultation. Chest x-ray is consistent with pulmonary edema. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. The patient dies despite appropriate medical care. Autopsy is performed and gross examination of the heart reveals uniformly thickened left ventricular walls with a small ventricular cavity. Histologic examination of the myocardial tissue reveals thick myocardial fibers with large, hyperchromatic nuclei as well as mild interstitial fibrosis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Cardiac amyloidosis is characterized on histopathology by extracellular, amorphous pink eosinophilic amyloid deposits abutting cardiomyocytes, and presents as restrictive cardiomyopathy with normal to thickened, stiff ventricular walls.
explanations.B: Prolonged systemic arterial hypertension imposes a chronic pressure overload on the left ventricle, causing concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. New sarcomeres are added in parallel, producing uniform circumferential LV wall thickening and a small LV cavity. On histology, cardiomyocytes demonstrate transverse enlargement with large, rectangular, hyperchromatic 'boxcar' nuclei and interstitial fibrosis. Loss of LV diastolic compliance predisposes to diastolic heart failure and pulmonary edema, especially triggered by the loss of atrial kick in new-onset atrial fibrillation.
explanations.C: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy features asymmetric septal hypertrophy (predominantly involving the subaortic interventricular septum) and marked myofiber disarray, rather than uniform concentric wall thickening.
explanations.D: Mitral stenosis obstructs LV filling, causing left atrial enlargement and pulmonary congestion without imposing a pressure load on the left ventricle.
explanations.E: Pulmonary arterial hypertension leads to pressure overload and concentric hypertrophy of the right ventricle, not the left ventricle.

generalExplanation: Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy is the classic cardiac adaptation to chronic pressure overload (most commonly systemic hypertension, followed by aortic stenosis). Sarcomeres synthesize and assemble in parallel, thickening the ventricular free wall and interventricular septum symmetrically while reducing LV luminal volume. On microscopic examination, enlarged hypertrophic cardiomyocytes exhibit enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei with mild interstitial collagenous fibrosis.
educationalObjective: Concentric left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy involves uniform thickening of the LV walls with reduction in LV cavity size and most commonly results from prolonged systemic hypertension. It can progress to hypertensive heart disease with impaired diastolic filling and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Histopathology demonstrates transverse thickening of cardiomyocytes with prominent hyperchromatic nuclei and interstitial fibrosis.

stem: A 44-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use came to the emergency department due to fever and chills. Multiple blood culture sets were positive for Staphylococcus aureus, and the patient was diagnosed with infective endocarditis. He was successfully treated with a long course of antibiotics. Six months later, he returns to the clinic for a follow-up evaluation. The patient has no symptoms and reports good exercise tolerance. He is afebrile, blood pressure is 140/62 mm Hg, pulse is 82/min, and respirations are 16/min. Chest auscultation reveals a decrescendo diastolic murmur over the third intercostal space along the left sternal border. Echocardiogram shows severe aortic regurgitation, likely as a sequela to the prior infection. Which of the following changes is most responsible for maintaining cardiac output in the setting of this valvular abnormality?

options.E: Increase in left ventricular stroke volume

explanations.A: Concentric LV hypertrophy occurs in response to pressure overload (hypertension, aortic stenosis); volume overload in aortic regurgitation triggers eccentric hypertrophy.
explanations.B: Left ventricular preload is substantially increased (not decreased) in AR due to backflow of regurgitant volume added to normal pulmonary venous return.
explanations.C: Aortic elasticity tends to decrease with age, but increased elasticity is not a compensatory cardiac mechanism.
explanations.D: Elevated afterload increases wall tension and accelerates cardiac decompensation, rather than helping maintain forward output.
explanations.E: In chronic aortic regurgitation (AR), diastolic runoff from the aorta back into the left ventricle creates progressive left ventricular volume overload. The LV accommodates by undergoing eccentric hypertrophy (addition of sarcomeres in series), which dilates the LV chamber and markedly increases total left ventricular stroke volume. This compensatory high stroke volume maintains effective forward cardiac output, allowing patients to remain asymptomatic for years.
explanations.F: Resting heart rate remains normal in chronic compensated AR; tachycardia is an acute, inadequate compensatory response seen in acute AR.

generalExplanation: In chronic aortic regurgitation, diastolic backflow of blood from the aorta dilates the left ventricle, causing eccentric hypertrophy. The expanded chamber volume increases end-diastolic sarcomere stretch (Frank-Starling law) and enables the left ventricle to eject a much higher total stroke volume with each contraction. Even though a portion of this stroke volume regurgitates back into the LV during diastole, the net forward stroke volume is sufficient to maintain normal resting cardiac output for years until eventual decompensation occurs.
educationalObjective: In chronic aortic regurgitation, persistent left ventricular volume overload triggers eccentric hypertrophy, which causes a compensatory increase in stroke volume to maintain cardiac output. This compensatory mechanism allows for a relatively long asymptomatic period in most patients; however, left ventricular dysfunction eventually occurs, leading to heart failure.

stem: A 50-year-old man is brought to the ER with severe dizziness and confusion. He states that he had an episode of chest pain and took several tablets of nitroglycerin. His current medications include a daily aspirin for heart attack prevention, an occasional acetaminophen for headaches and occasionally tadalafil for erectile dysfunction. His blood pressure is 50/20 mmHg and his heart rate is 120 beats/min. Which of the following cellular changes is most likely responsible for this patient's symptoms?

explanations.A: Receptor downregulation accounts for tolerance or tachyphylaxis (eg, with continuous nitrate infusion or opioids), not acute synergistic hypotension.
explanations.B: Gs protein activates adenylyl cyclase to increase cyclic AMP, which is not the pathway targeted by nitrates or PDE inhibitors.
explanations.C: Nitrates are metabolized to nitric oxide (NO), which stimulates soluble guanylate cyclase to produce cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP). Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors (eg, tadalafil, sildenafil) block the enzymatic degradation of cGMP to GMP in vascular smooth muscle. Combining nitrates with PDE-5 inhibitors produces massive, synergistic intracellular accumulation of cGMP, causing profound smooth muscle relaxation, widespread peripheral vasodilation, and severe, life-threatening hypotension and reflex tachycardia.
explanations.D: Receptor tyrosine kinases mediate insulin and growth factor signaling.
explanations.E: Enhanced phospholipid metabolism involves the Gq-phospholipase C-IP3/DAG pathway, which increases intracellular calcium and promotes vasoconstriction.
explanations.F: Nitrate tolerance is avoided with nitrate-free intervals, but acute severe hypotension represents lethal drug synergy rather than tolerance.

generalExplanation: Co-administration of organic nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide mononitrate) and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) is strictly contraindicated. Nitrates increase cGMP synthesis via NO-activated guanylyl cyclase, while PDE-5 inhibitors inhibit cGMP breakdown. The resulting unchecked accumulation of intracellular cGMP in vascular smooth muscle causes profound dephosphorylation of myosin light chains, inducing systemic vasodilation, precipitous refractory hypotension, and cardiogenic collapse.
educationalObjective: Using nitrates together with phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitors used for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension causes a profound systemic hypotension because they both increase intracellular cGMP which causes vascular smooth muscle relaxation. Their use together is absolutely contraindicated.

stem: A 78-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to lightheadedness that began earlier in the day. This morning, the patient felt unsteady and almost passed out when he tried to get out of bed. He has not had similar symptoms before and he has had no chest pain or shortness of breath. He has a history of coronary artery disease requiring percutaneous coronary intervention. The rhythm strip of the ECG obtained in the emergency department shows regular sinus P waves marching at ~75/min and completely independent, regular narrow QRS complexes marching slowly at ~30/min with no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?

options.A: Degenerative changes involving the atrioventricular node
options.B: Degenerative changes involving the sinus node
options.C: Ectopic electrical foci in left ventricular myocardium
options.D: Reentrant circuit involving the cavotricuspid isthmus

explanations.A: The ECG strip demonstrates complete (third-degree) atrioventricular (AV) block. There is complete AV dissociation: regular P waves march out at the intrinsic rate of the SA node (~75/min), while independent QRS complexes fire at a slow escape rate (<40/min). In an elderly patient, third-degree AV block is most commonly caused by age-related sclerosis and degenerative calcification/fibrosis of the AV conduction system (Lenègre or Lev disease) or chronic ischemic heart disease.
explanations.B: Degenerative disease of the SA node causes sick sinus syndrome (sinus pauses, sinus arrest), where dropped P waves occur but P waves are followed by QRS complexes when present.
explanations.C: Ectopic ventricular foci cause ventricular premature complexes or ventricular tachycardia (wide, rapid QRS complexes).
explanations.D: A reentrant circuit in the cavotricuspid isthmus produces atrial flutter with characteristic saw-toothed flutter waves.
explanations.E: Sporadic depolarization of multiple atrial foci causes atrial fibrillation, with an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm and absence of distinct P waves.

generalExplanation: Third-degree (complete) AV block occurs when no supraventricular impulses are conducted from the atria to the ventricles. Cardiac pacemaking splits into two independent pacemakers: the sinoatrial node drives the atria (producing regular P waves), while an escape pacemaker in the AV junction (narrow QRS, 40–55 bpm) or in the His-Purkinje/ventricular system (wide QRS, 20–40 bpm) drives the ventricles. Complete heart block causes marked bradycardia, reduced cardiac output, presyncope, and syncope (Stokes-Adams attacks), requiring permanent pacemaker implantation.
educationalObjective: Third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block involves dysfunction of the atrioventricular node, resulting in total lack of communication between the atria and ventricles. On ECG, there is dissociation of P waves and QRS complexes, with P waves marching out at the intrinsic rate of the sinoatrial node and QRS complexes at the intrinsic rate of the His bundle or ventricles (escape rhythm).

stem: A 53-year-old man comes to the emergency department with shortness of breath and chest tightness. The patient was playing in a poker tournament when his symptoms first began. He has a history of hypertension and is not compliant with his medications. His last medical follow-up was a year ago. Blood pressure is 195/115 mm Hg and pulse is 90/min and regular. Lung examination reveals bibasilar crackles. Nitroglycerin infusion is started and results in significant symptomatic improvement. Repeat blood pressure is 165/90 mm Hg. Which of the following intracellular events is most likely responsible for the beneficial effects of this patient's treatment?

explanations.A: Actin is not directly phosphorylated during smooth muscle relaxation; smooth muscle tone is regulated by the phosphorylation state of the regulatory myosin light chains.
explanations.B: Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum increases free cytosolic calcium, activating myosin light-chain kinase to promote smooth muscle contraction.
explanations.C: Nitrates promote synthesis, not degradation, of cyclic mononucleotides (cGMP). Phosphodiesterase enzymes degrade cGMP.
explanations.D: IP3 increases intracellular calcium, stimulating contraction and vasoconstriction.
explanations.E: Nitroglycerin is converted to nitric oxide (NO) in vascular smooth muscle cells, which activates soluble guanylate cyclase to synthesize cGMP from GTP. Elevated cGMP activates myosin light-chain phosphatase (MLCP) and reduces cytosolic calcium. MLCP dephosphorylates the regulatory myosin light chains, preventing cross-bridge cycling with actin and causing vascular smooth muscle relaxation and venodilation.
explanations.F: Tyrosine kinase activation mediates signaling of peptide hormones like insulin and growth factors, but is not involved in nitrate vasodilation.

generalExplanation:
Mechanism of nitrate-induced vascular relaxation:
1. Nitrates are denitrated intracellularly to yield nitric oxide (NO).
2. NO stimulates soluble guanylate cyclase, increasing intracellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP).
3. cGMP promotes calcium extrusion and uptake, lowering cytosolic free Ca2+.
4. cGMP activates myosin light-chain phosphatase, which dephosphorylates myosin light chains.
5. Dephosphorylated myosin cannot bind actin filaments, resulting in vascular smooth muscle relaxation and preferential venodilation.
educationalObjective: Nitrates (via conversion to nitric oxide) activate guanylate cyclase and increase intracellular levels of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP). Increased levels of cGMP lead to myosin light-chain dephosphorylation, resulting in vascular smooth muscle relaxation.

stem: Physiologists conduct a series of experiments on hypophysectomized animals to investigate the effects of cortisol on vascular reactivity. Their initial tests show that administration of cortisol alone does not elicit a vascular response. Next, the researchers measure vascular reactivity to an infusion of norepinephrine both with and without pretreatment with cortisol. The results show that norepinephrine alone causes a modest vasoconstrictive response, while pretreatment with cortisol markedly potentiates the vasoconstrictive response to norepinephrine. Which of the following pharmacologic principles best describes the effect of cortisol in this experiment?

explanations.A: An additive effect occurs when two drugs with individual active effects produce a combined effect equal to the arithmetic sum of their individual actions (1 + 1 = 2). Cortisol has no intrinsic vasoactive effect on its own (0 + 1 > 1).
explanations.B: Alterations in drug metabolism involve hepatic enzyme induction or inhibition (eg, CYP450 modulation), not direct receptor upregulation.
explanations.C: Permissiveness describes a pharmacologic phenomenon in which a hormone or agent has no direct physiological effect on a process when administered alone, but its presence is required for another hormone to exert its maximal biological efficacy (0 + 1 > 1). Cortisol exerts a permissive effect on vascular reactivity by upregulating alpha-1 adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle, allowing catecholamines to elicit maximal vasoconstriction.
explanations.D: A synergistic effect occurs when two active agents each produce an effect, and their combination exceeds the sum of their individual effects (1 + 1 > 2). Because cortisol alone has no vasoconstrictive effect, the phenomenon is classified as permissiveness rather than synergism.
explanations.E: Tachyphylaxis describes the rapid diminution of responsiveness following repeated drug administration (acute tolerance).

generalExplanation:
Cortisol exhibits classic permissive actions in multiple physiological systems:
1. Vascular tone: Upregulates vascular alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, permitting catecholamines and angiotensin II to induce maximal vasoconstriction (in adrenal insufficiency, loss of this permissive effect contributes to refractory hypotension).
2. Bronchodilation: Potentiates beta-2 adrenergic receptor-mediated relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle.
3. Metabolism: Potentiates glucagon- and epinephrine-stimulated hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.
educationalObjective: A permissive hormone has no effect on a physiologic process by itself but allows another hormone to exert its maximal effect on that process. Cortisol exerts a permissive effect on catecholamines to potentiate vasoconstriction and bronchodilation; it also has a permissive effect on glucagon to increase glucose release from the liver.

stem: A 45-year-old man comes to the hospital with acute onset of severe chest pain and diaphoresis. The patient describes the pain as "squeezing," different from any discomfort he has ever had. He has a past medical history of hypertension, and his father underwent coronary artery bypass grafting at age 50. The patient is diagnosed with acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction and undergoes an urgent coronary intervention with stent placement into the right coronary artery. He is also started on high-intensity atorvastatin therapy, along with antiplatelet therapy and appropriate medications to control blood pressure. Four weeks later, the patient's total cholesterol level is 140 mg/dL, down from 200 mg/dL before discharge. Which of the following has most likely increased as the result of the therapy?

explanations.A: ApoB-100 is the primary structural apolipoprotein on VLDL and LDL particles; as statins enhance clearance of LDL and VLDL, circulating ApoB-100 levels decrease.
explanations.B: Biliary cholesterol excretion decreases because statins inhibit de novo hepatic cholesterol synthesis.
explanations.C: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) block the intracellular rate-limiting step of cholesterol biosynthesis. The resulting depletion of intrahepatic cholesterol stimulates sterol regulatory element-binding protein 2 (SREBP-2), leading to increased transcription and upregulation of cell-surface LDL receptor density on hepatocytes. This dramatically increases endocytic clearance of circulating atherogenic LDL particles from the bloodstream.
explanations.D: Statins do not increase plasma free fatty acid levels.
explanations.E: VLDL synthesis and secretion by the liver are decreased following statin therapy.

generalExplanation: Statins competitive inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, preventing the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate. Intracellular cholesterol depletion prompts hepatocytes to upregulate transcription of the low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor gene via SREBP-2. The marked increase in surface LDL receptor density accelerates receptor-mediated endocytosis of circulating LDL and VLDL remnants, clearing them from plasma and lowering circulating LDL levels by 20%–50%.
educationalObjective: Treatment with statins causes hepatocytes to increase their LDL receptor density, leading to increased uptake of circulating LDL.

stem: A 19-year-old man comes to the office due to difficulty seeing and blurred vision, which have worsened slowly over the past year. He is a second-year college student pursuing a degree in biochemistry. His grades are excellent, but he is concerned about the effect his poor vision has had on his classes this semester. The patient is also an avid swimmer. He weighs 71 kg (156.5 lb) and is 195 cm (6 ft 5 in) tall. Physical examination shows tall, slender build with increased arm-to-height ratio, arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum, joint hypermobility, flat feet, and upward lens dislocation (ectopia lentis). This patient is most likely to die from which of the following conditions?

explanations.A: The patient has Marfan syndrome (autosomal dominant mutation in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15 encoding fibrillin-1). Defective fibrillin-1 disrupts microfibril assembly and extracellular matrix scaffolding, weakening elastic tissues. The most life-threatening manifestations involve the cardiovascular system: cystic medial degeneration of the aorta leads to progressive aortic root dilation, aortic regurgitation, and type A aortic dissection or rupture, which is the leading cause of death in Marfan syndrome.
explanations.B: Liver disease is not associated with Marfan syndrome.
explanations.C: Premature myocardial infarction and thromboembolic strokes are characteristic of homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency), which shares a marfanoid habitus but is distinguished by intellectual disability and downward lens dislocation.
explanations.D: Immunodeficiency and overwhelming infections are not features of Marfan syndrome.
explanations.E: Renal failure is not a primary complication of Marfan syndrome.

generalExplanation: Marfan syndrome results from heterozygous mutations in FBN1, which encodes fibrillin-1 (a glycoprotein component of microfibrils that sheathe elastin fibers). Hallmark skeletal features include arachnodactyly, scoliosis, pectus deformities, and tall stature; ocular features include upward/outward ectopia lentis. Cardiovascular involvement is the main determinant of mortality, specifically cystic medial necrosis of the ascending aorta leading to aneurysmal dilation, aortic valve insufficiency, and fatal aortic dissection or rupture.
educationalObjective: Cardiovascular lesions are the most life-threatening complications associated with Marfan syndrome. Early-onset cystic medial degeneration of the aorta predisposes to aortic dissection, the most common cause of death in these patients.

stem: A 60-year-old man comes to the emergency department with dizziness and palpitations. He woke up this morning with an intermittent pounding sensation in his chest. The patient has occasionally experienced a similar sensation in the past and did not think it was serious. Later, while mowing the lawn, he became lightheaded and had to sit down to avoid passing out. After receiving the appropriate workup, the patient is diagnosed with a cardiac arrhythmia and started on a medication known to prolong the QT interval. However, the drug is associated with a lower incidence of torsade de pointes than other QT-prolonging agents. Which of the following medications was most likely used in this patient?

explanations.A: Adenosine slows AV nodal conduction via A1 purinergic receptors and has an ultra-short half-life (<10 seconds); it does not prolong the QT interval.
explanations.B: Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic that inhibits outward potassium channels (delayed rectifier K+ current) during phase 3 repolarization, causing significant prolongation of the ventricular action potential duration and QT interval on ECG. Uniquely, unlike other class III drugs (sotalol, dofetilide) or class IA drugs (quinidine, procainamide), amiodarone causes homogeneous repolarization across myocardial layers (minimal transmural dispersion of repolarization) and possesses mild beta- and calcium-blocking properties, making torsades de pointes extremely rare (<1%).
explanations.C: Digoxin shortens the QT interval and produces downsloping 'scooped' ST depressions.
explanations.D: Esmolol is an ultra-short-acting beta-blocker (class II) that slows AV nodal conduction without prolonging the QT interval.
explanations.E: Lidocaine (class IB) blocks sodium channels with fast dissociation kinetics and actually shortens the ventricular action potential duration and QT interval.
explanations.F: Procainamide (class IA) prolongs the action potential duration and carries a substantial risk of inducing torsades de pointes.
explanations.G: Verapamil (class IV) slows AV conduction and prolongs the PR interval, but does not prolong the QT interval.

generalExplanation: Class III antiarrhythmics predominantly inhibit outward delayed rectifier potassium currents, prolonging phase 3 repolarization and the QT interval. In most agents, non-uniform prolongation of repolarization between epicardial, endocardial, and M cells generates increased transmural dispersion of repolarization, predisposing to early afterdepolarizations and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (torsades de pointes). Amiodarone is an exception: it prolongs the action potential homogeneously across all myocardial layers and exerts additional class I, II, and IV antiarrhythmic effects, making torsades de pointes extraordinarily uncommon despite marked QT prolongation.
educationalObjective: Amiodarone (and other class III and class IA antiarrhythmic agents) causes lengthening of the cardiac action potential, which manifests as QT interval prolongation on ECG. QT prolongation caused by amiodarone, in contrast to other drugs, is associated with a very low risk of torsades de pointes.

stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the office by his parents for evaluation of cyanosis with minimal exertion. The boy has had occasional episodes of "turning blue" that first began during infancy and are now occurring more frequently. During the episodes, the boy assumes a squatting position as it makes him "feel better." The family recently immigrated to the United States; the boy has never had a medical checkup prior to this visit. Physical examination reveals a prominent right ventricular impulse and a harsh systolic murmur. Which of the following embryological events is the most likely mechanism that caused this patient's condition?

options.E: Linear development of the aorticopulmonary septum

explanations.A: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return results from failure of the common pulmonary vein to incorporate into the left atrium.
explanations.B: Aortic arch constriction leads to coarctation of the aorta, presenting with upper-to-lower extremity blood pressure discrepancies and lower extremity claudication.
explanations.C: Tetralogy of Fallot (ToF) results embryologically from anterior and superior (cephalad) deviation of the infundibular (conal) septum during cardiogenesis. This single developmental defect causes the four hallmark anomalies: (1) infundibular pulmonic stenosis, (2) malalignment ventricular septal defect, (3) overriding aorta, and (4) secondary right ventricular hypertrophy.
explanations.D: Endocardial cushion defects result in atrioventricular canal defects (primum ASD, VSD, common AV valve), strongly associated with Down syndrome.
explanations.E: Linear rather than spiral partitioning of the truncus arteriosus by the aorticopulmonary septum results in transposition of the great arteries (TGA).

generalExplanation: Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease beyond infancy. It is caused by abnormal neural crest cell migration that causes anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular septum. The degree of right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction dictates the severity of symptoms and the volume of right-to-left shunting across the VSD. Squatting acutely increases systemic vascular resistance (afterload), which elevates left ventricular pressure above right ventricular pressure, reversing the shunt from right-to-left to left-to-right and augmenting pulmonary blood flow.
educationalObjective: Tetralogy of Fallot results from anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular septum during embryologic development, resulting in a malaligned ventricular septal defect (VSD) with an overriding aorta. As a result, the patient has right ventricular outflow obstruction (resulting in a systolic murmur) and squats to increase the peripheral systemic vascular resistance (afterload) and decrease right-to-left shunting across the VSD.

stem:
Cardiac catheterization is performed on a 7-year-old boy. The report reveals the following oxygen saturation pattern in the cardiac chambers and outflow tracts:
- Superior vena cava: 70%
- Right atrium: 70%
- Right ventricle: 81%
- Pulmonary artery: 81%
- Pulmonary veins: 96%
- Left atrium: 96%
- Left ventricle: 96%
- Aorta: 96%

This patient most likely has which of the following findings on physical examination?

options.A: Bifid carotid pulse with brisk upstroke
options.B: Continuous murmur over the upper precordium
options.D: Fixed splitting of S2 on cardiac auscultation
options.E: Holosystolic murmur over the left sternal border

explanations.A: A bifid 'spike-and-dome' carotid pulse is characteristic of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.
explanations.B: A continuous machine-like murmur is classic for patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), which shows an oxygen step-up isolated to the pulmonary artery (PA saturation > RV saturation).
explanations.C: Decreased femoral-to-brachial blood pressure ratio is typical of coarctation of the aorta.
explanations.D: Fixed, wide splitting of S2 is the hallmark of an atrial septal defect (ASD), which causes an oxygen step-up at the right atrium (RA saturation > SVC saturation).
explanations.E: An oxygen saturation step-up from 70% in the right atrium to 81% in the right ventricle indicates an intracardiac left-to-right shunt at the ventricular level, pathognomonic for a ventricular septal defect (VSD). Small, hemodynamically restrictive VSDs create high-velocity turbulent blood flow across the defect during systole, generating a loud, harsh holosystolic murmur loudest at the left mid-to-lower sternal border.
explanations.F: Cyanosis and digital clubbing develop when chronic pulmonary hypertension causes shunt reversal (Eisenmenger syndrome), which would decrease left ventricular and aortic saturation.

generalExplanation:
Cardiac oximetry series assessment:
- Right atrium (70%) receives desaturated systemic venous return.
- Right ventricle shows an abrupt jump to 81% (step-up >7% indicates a significant left-to-right shunt).
- Pulmonary artery maintains the elevated 81% saturation.
- Left heart chambers and aorta remain normally oxygenated at 96%.
This physiological pattern establishes a ventricular septal defect (VSD), the most common congenital heart anomaly. A restrictive VSD causes a prominent holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border.
educationalObjective: Increased blood oxygen saturation between 2 right-sided vessels or chambers indicates the presence of a left-to-right shunt. If the abnormal oxygen increase occurs between the right atrium and the right ventricle, a ventricular septal defect (VSD) is likely present. Small VSDs produce a holosystolic murmur that is loudest over the lower left sternal border.

stem: A 56-year-old woman comes to clinic for follow-up of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. In the last 3 months, the patient has been hospitalized twice due to acute decompensation of heart failure that required treatment with intravenous furosemide. Since her most recent discharge, she has been taking high doses of oral furosemide, but she continues to have progressive lower extremity edema and weight gain. Serum creatinine is 1.2 mg/dL and serum potassium is 4.1 mEq/L. The addition of metolazone may assist in treating this patient because of which of the following effects of loop diuretics?

options.A: Increased calcium delivery to the distal tubules
options.B: Increased sodium delivery to the distal tubules
options.D: Increased tubular reabsorption of uric acid

explanations.A: Although loop diuretics reduce calcium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, calcium delivery does not regulate systemic extracellular fluid volume.
explanations.B: Loop diuretics (eg, furosemide) inhibit the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, resulting in delivery of large amounts of sodium and chloride to the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). Over time, the distal tubule hypertrophies and upregulates Na-Cl cotransporter (NCCT) activity, reabsorbing much of the excess delivered sodium and blunting loop diuretic efficacy (diuretic resistance). Adding a thiazide diuretic such as metolazone selectively blocks the Na-Cl cotransporter in the DCT, preventing compensatory distal sodium reabsorption and producing potent sequential nephron blockade with marked synergistic diuresis.
explanations.C: Metabolic alkalosis can occur, but carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (not thiazides) target bicarbonate handling.
explanations.D: Loop and thiazide diuretics cause hyperuricemia, which is an adverse effect rather than a therapeutic target.
explanations.E: Glucose reabsorption is mediated by SGLT2 in the early proximal tubule, not affected by loop diuretics.
explanations.F: Loop diuretics decrease potassium reabsorption, but potassium excretion is not the reason metolazone improves fluid removal.

generalExplanation: In refractory congestive heart failure with persistent volume overload, high-dose loop diuretic monotherapy often triggers adaptive hypertrophy and increased sodium transport in the distal convoluted tubule, limiting overall natriuresis. Metolazone is a potent thiazide-like diuretic that acts on the distal convoluted tubule by inhibiting the Na+/Cl- cotransporter. Administering metolazone alongside furosemide achieves synergistic 'sequential nephron blockade', simultaneously eliminating sodium reabsorption in both the thick ascending limb and the distal convoluted tubule.
educationalObjective: Thiazide diuretics, especially metolazone, potentiate the diuretic effect of loop diuretics (eg, furosemide) by blocking the reabsorption of the increased distal tubular sodium delivery caused by loop diuretics.

stem: A 61-year-old woman is hospitalized due to chest pressure and shortness of breath. Two days ago her husband died in a car accident. The patient's medical history is significant for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and gout. Five years ago, she was diagnosed with breast cancer and treated with surgery and chemotherapy. Blood pressure is 165/90 mm Hg and pulse is 95/min and regular. Physical examination is unremarkable. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with T-wave inversions in the anterior leads. Echocardiogram shows hypokinesis of the apical wall with decreased left ventricular ejection fraction. Diagnostic coronary angiography shows no evidence of obstructive coronary artery disease. The patient is treated medically and discharged home. Four weeks later, she is seen in the office and has no symptoms. Repeat echocardiography demonstrates normal left ventricular wall motion and ejection fraction. Which of the following is the likely cause of this patient's initial presentation?

options.C: Myocardial hypertrophy and fibrosis due to uncontrolled hypertension

explanations.A: The clinical scenario is classic for stress-induced (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy ('broken heart syndrome'), which characteristically affects postmenopausal women following intense acute physical or emotional stress. A massive surge of endogenous catecholamines causes microvascular coronary spasm, direct cellular calcium overload, and metabolic stunning of the myocardium. Echocardiography classically shows transient hypokinesis or akinesis of the mid and apical LV segments with basal hypercontractility, creating apical ballooning resembling a Japanese octopus trap (takotsubo). Left ventricular function completely normalizes within 4 to 8 weeks.
explanations.B: Coronary angiography demonstrated normal epicardial coronaries without obstructive atherosclerotic stenosis or occlusive thrombosis.
explanations.C: Hypertensive heart disease causes concentric LV hypertrophy and chronic diastolic dysfunction without acute reversible apical ballooning.
explanations.D: Lymphocytic myocarditis causes viral dilated cardiomyopathy with global hypokinesis that persists for months or permanently.
explanations.E: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity causes irreversible, dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy with myofibrillar loss and vacuolization, not acute reversible apical ballooning.

generalExplanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (stress-induced cardiomyopathy, apical ballooning syndrome) is triggered by an acute surge in circulating catecholamines during profound emotional or physical distress. The hyperadrenergic state induces direct cardiomyocyte toxicity and epicardial/microvascular coronary spasm, culminating in transient apical and mid-ventricular hypokinesis with hypercontractile basal segments. Despite presenting with symptoms, ECG changes, and troponin elevations mimicking acute anterior STEMI, coronary angiography reveals patent arteries, and cardiac systolic function recovers completely with supportive medical management.
educationalObjective: Stress-induced (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy is characterized by hypokinesis of the mid and apical segments and hyperkinesis of the basal segments of the left ventricle, resulting in systolic dysfunction. The condition is likely caused by a surge of catecholamines in the setting of physical or emotional stress. It usually affects postmenopausal women and resolves on its own within several weeks.

stem: A 10-year-old immigrant from Eastern Europe is brought to the office due to exertional dyspnea and fatigability. The boy tires easily when walking and cannot keep up with his peers at the playground. According to his parents, he was diagnosed with congenital heart disease in infancy, but corrective surgery was unavailable. They cannot recall the details of his diagnosis. He takes a daily multivitamin and no medications. Pulse oximetry of the right hand shows 99% on room air. Physical examination shows a 3/6 systolic murmur and mild, bilateral cyanosis and clubbing of the toes. Examination of the fingers is normal. All extremity pulses are full and equal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: An atrial septal defect with Eisenmenger syndrome shunts deoxygenated blood into the left heart chambers before the brachiocephalic and subclavian origins, causing equal, generalized cyanosis and clubbing of both upper and lower extremities.
explanations.B: The pathognomonic physical finding in this patient is differential cyanosis and clubbing (cyanosis and clubbing limited to the lower extremities with normal, pink upper extremities and normal right hand oxygen saturation). This finding is uniquely caused by an uncorrected large patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) that has progressed to Eisenmenger syndrome. The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta DISTAL to the origin of the left subclavian artery. Consequently, fully oxygenated blood from the left ventricle perfuses the head and upper extremities via the brachiocephalic, carotid, and subclavian arteries, while deoxygenated blood shunted right-to-left across the PDA travels down the descending aorta to supply the lower extremities.
explanations.C: Tetralogy of Fallot produces generalized, whole-body cyanosis affecting both fingers and toes equally.
explanations.D: Transposition of the great arteries without surgical switch causes profound neonatal cyanosis that is incompatible with survival to age 10 without major interventions.
explanations.E: Ventricular septal defect with Eisenmenger syndrome introduces deoxygenated blood into the left ventricle, distributing desaturated blood to all aortic branches equally and causing generalized cyanosis.

generalExplanation: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) normally shunts blood left-to-right from the high-pressure aorta into the low-pressure pulmonary artery. Over years, high pulmonary blood flow causes medial hypertrophy and intimal proliferation of pulmonary arterioles (pulmonary vascular remodeling), eventually raising pulmonary vascular resistance above systemic resistance. The resulting reversal of flow (right-to-left shunt, Eisenmenger syndrome) delivers desaturated blood into the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery. Because cephalic and upper extremity vessels arise proximal to the ductus, the head and arms receive oxygenated blood (normal fingers, 99% SaO2), whereas the descending aorta delivers hypoxic blood to the lower body (cyanotic, clubbed toes).
educationalObjective: Lower extremity differential clubbing and cyanosis without pulse discrepancy is caused by a large patent ductus arteriosus complicated by Eisenmenger syndrome (reversal of shunt flow from left-to-right to right-to-left). In contrast, intracardiac right-to-left shunting in patients with large septal defects and Tetralogy of Fallot results in whole-body cyanosis.

stem: A 1-week-old boy is brought to the office for his first primary care visit following an uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 40 weeks gestation. The boy was born to a 30-year-old woman who took prenatal vitamins throughout the pregnancy. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus at 28 weeks gestation, which was treated with dietary modification and exercise. The nursery course was uncomplicated, and the boy was discharged at around 30 hours of life following observation of appropriate breastfeeding, voiding, and stooling. His weight, length, and head circumference are at the 50th percentile. Physical examination shows a grade II/VI harsh, holosystolic murmur best heard at the left mid to lower sternal border. Birth records show that no murmur was heard by 2 different health care providers in the newborn nursery. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Coarctation of the aorta typically presents with weak or delayed femoral pulses and upper extremity hypertension.
explanations.B: Ebstein's anomaly features downward displacement of tricuspid leaflets into the RV, presenting with cyanosis and severe tricuspid regurgitation.
explanations.C: Patent ductus arteriosus produces a continuous, 'machinery-like' murmur best heard in the left infraclavicular area.
explanations.D: Peripheral pulmonic stenosis produces a soft, mid-systolic ejection murmur radiating to the axillae and back.
explanations.E: Primum ASD is accompanied by a fixed split S2 and mitral regurgitation.
explanations.F: Secundum ASD causes a wide, fixed splitting of S2 and a systolic ejection murmur across the pulmonic valve.
explanations.G: Tetralogy of Fallot presents with an ejection systolic murmur of pulmonic stenosis and episodic cyanosis.
explanations.H: WPW syndrome is an electrophysiologic arrhythmia substrate and does not cause a cardiac murmur.
explanations.I: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart anomaly. In the immediate newborn nursery period (first 24–48 hours of life), high fetal pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is still elevated and approximately equal to systemic vascular resistance, so minimal trans-septal pressure gradient exists and no murmur is audible. Over the first 1 to 2 weeks of life, as the pulmonary vascular resistance normally declines, the left-to-right pressure gradient progressively increases, generating high-velocity turbulent flow across the defect that manifests as a new, loud, blowing holosystolic murmur loudest at the left lower sternal border.

generalExplanation: A ventricular septal defect produces a classic harsh holosystolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border. Importantly, this murmur is typically absent at birth because physiological neonate pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is near systemic vascular resistance, limiting trans-defect flow. As the infant breathes room air and pulmonary arteriolar smooth muscle relaxes, PVR drops substantially over the first 4 to 10 days of life, unmasking vigorous left-to-right shunting and causing the murmur to become clinically prominent at the 1-to-2-week well-child check.
educationalObjective: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) typically presents in the neonatal period after pulmonary vascular resistance has declined. The clinical presentation depends on the size of the defect, which ranges from an asymptomatic holosystolic murmur (small VSD) to heart failure (large VSD).

stem: A 32-year-old man comes to the office due to progressive dyspnea, dizziness, and chest discomfort. He has no prior medical problems but had a mild respiratory illness 2 weeks earlier that resolved spontaneously. His father has a history of myocardial infarction. Echocardiogram shows pericardial fluid accumulation with late diastolic collapse of the right atrium. Which of the following physical examination findings is most likely to be seen in this patient?

options.B: Drop in pulse amplitude during inspiration
options.D: Rapidly rising pulse with high amplitude

explanations.A: Pulsus alternans (beat-to-beat alteration in pulse amplitude) occurs in severe left ventricular systolic failure. Electrical alternans on ECG describes shifting QRS amplitudes as the heart swings in fluid.
explanations.B: The patient has acute cardiac tamponade due to viral pericarditis with pericardial effusion. A hallmark physical finding of cardiac tamponade is pulsus paradoxus, defined as an exaggerated decrease (>10 mm Hg) in systolic blood pressure during inspiration, detectable palpably as a palpable drop or disappearance in peripheral arterial pulse amplitude during inspiration. In normal physiology, inspiration increases systemic venous return to the right heart, which expands into the pericardial space. In tamponade, the rigid, fluid-filled pericardium prevents free-wall expansion, forcing the interventricular septum to bow leftward into the left ventricle. This reduces LV diastolic filling, stroke volume, and systolic arterial pressure during inspiration.
explanations.C: A dicrotic pulse (two distinct peaks per cardiac cycle) is seen in patients with severe heart failure and high systemic vascular resistance.
explanations.D: A hyperkinetic, bounding pulse (water-hammer/Corrigan pulse) is characteristic of aortic regurgitation or high-output states.
explanations.E: A slow-rising, low-amplitude pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) is characteristic of severe valvular aortic stenosis.

generalExplanation: Cardiac tamponade impairs ventricular diastolic filling due to elevated intrapericardial hydrostatic pressure. Classic clinical findings include Beck's triad (hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled heart sounds) and pulsus paradoxus. Pulsus paradoxus is an abnormally large drop in systolic blood pressure (>10 mm Hg) and palpable decline in pulse volume during inspiration caused by respiratory ventricular interdependence, where increased right ventricular filling causes the interventricular septum to bulge leftward into the LV chamber, reducing stroke volume.
educationalObjective: Pulsus paradoxus refers to an exaggerated drop (>10 mm Hg) in systolic blood pressure during inspiration. It is most commonly seen in patients with cardiac tamponade but can also occur in severe asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypovolemic shock, and constrictive pericarditis.

stem: A 54-year-old Caucasian male comes to the emergency room with retrosternal chest pain of 30 minutes duration. The patient also complains of sweating and mild dyspnea. A single tablet of nitroglycerin is delivered sublingually, and the patient's pain decreases significantly. The patient has experienced several similar episodes of pain over the last 12 hours, all of which resolved spontaneously. Which of the following ultrastructural changes would most likely indicate irreversible myocardial cell injury in this patient?

explanations.A: Myofibril relaxation occurs rapidly (within 60 seconds) after ischemia onset due to rapid depletion of ATP, representing reversible injury.
explanations.B: Detachment and disaggregation of ribosomes from the rough endoplasmic reticulum reflects reversible cellular swelling and ATP reduction.
explanations.C: Mitochondrial vacuolization, disruption of cristae, and appearance of large amorphous calcium- and phospholipid-rich flocculent densities within the mitochondrial matrix indicate irreversible cellular necrosis. Once the inner mitochondrial membrane loses integrity, the cell permanently loses the capacity to generate ATP via oxidative phosphorylation, marking the point of no return.
explanations.D: Disaggregation of nuclear granular elements and chromatin clumping occur during early reversible ischemia due to intracellular acidosis.
explanations.E: Intracellular lipid vacuole accumulation is a feature of reversible fatty change.
explanations.F: Rapid depletion of glycogen granules begins within minutes as anaerobic glycolysis accelerates, reflecting reversible ischemic change.

generalExplanation: In myocardial ischemia, reversible cellular injury occurs within the first 20 to 30 minutes and includes depletion of cellular glycogen, ATP breakdown, intracellular lactic acidosis with chromatin clumping, cellular and endoplasmic reticulum swelling, ribosome detachment, and loss of cardiomyocyte contractility (myofibrillar relaxation). Irreversible injury is defined ultrastructurally by permanent plasma membrane disruption and severe mitochondrial structural damage—namely mitochondrial swelling, matrix vacuolization, and deposition of large amorphous matrix densities.
educationalObjective: Mitochondrial vacuolization is typically a sign of irreversible cell injury, signifying that the involved mitochondria are permanently unable to generate ATP.

stem: Autopsy of a 78-year-old man demonstrates decreased left ventricular cavity size and a sigmoid-shaped ventricular septum. Light microscopy shows increased collagen content within the ventricular wall. Some myocardial cells also have brownish perinuclear cytoplasmic inclusions. The changes described are most consistent with which of the following conditions?

explanations.A: Dilated cardiomyopathy produces marked biventricular enlargement and eccentric dilation, not a reduced LV cavity.
explanations.B: Chronic hemolytic anemia causes systemic iron overload (hemosiderosis) with Prussian-blue-positive coarse iron granules, leading to dilated or restrictive cardiomyopathy.
explanations.C: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy features marked myofiber disarray and severe septal thickening in young adults, not lipofuscin accumulation in an asymptomatic elderly patient.
explanations.D: Ischemic cardiomyopathy typically causes patchy subendocardial vacuolization and myocardial infarction scars.
explanations.E: Long-standing hypertension causes concentric LV hypertrophy with enlarged cardiomyocyte nuclei, but lacks the hallmark lipofuscin accumulation of senescence.
explanations.F: Normal cardiovascular aging is characterized morphologically by: (1) a reduction in left ventricular base-to-apex long-axis dimension, causing the ventricular septum to bulge into the LV outflow tract in a classic 'sigmoid shape'; (2) myocardial atrophy accompanied by increased interstitial collagen and amyloid deposition; and (3) intracellular accumulation of brown, perinuclear granules of lipofuscin (an insoluble 'wear-and-tear' pigment derived from lipid peroxidation of autophagocytosed membranes).

generalExplanation: Normal age-related cardiac remodeling involves characteristic gross and microscopic changes: gross inspection shows a decrease in the base-to-apex LV dimension with relative transverse dilation of the ascending aorta, which imparts a curved, sigmoid appearance to the basilar ventricular septum. Histologically, there is loss of myocytes with compensatory hypertrophy of remaining fibers, increased interstitial collagen, and accumulation of brownish perinuclear lipofuscin pigment representing oxidized subcellular lipid polymers.
educationalObjective: Normal morphological changes in the aging heart include a decrease in left ventricular chamber apex-to-base dimension, development of a sigmoid-shaped ventricular septum, myocardial atrophy with increased collagen deposition, and accumulation of cytoplasmic lipofuscin pigment within cardiomyocytes.

stem: A 23-year-old previously healthy man is brought to the emergency department after a stab injury. His friends report that they were "walking down the street minding our own business when a guy jumped out in front of us from behind a dumpster and stabbed him in the chest." They were able to disarm the man after this single attack, and the man then ran off into an alley. The patient is conscious but in distress. Physical examination shows a laterally directed anterior chest wall stab wound at the fifth intercostal space along the left midclavicular line. Which of the following structures is most likely to have been injured in this patient?

explanations.A: The azygos vein runs in the posterior mediastinum immediately to the right of the vertebral column.
explanations.B: The inferior vena cava courses through the right posterior mediastinum and enters the right atrium.
explanations.C: The left atrium forms the most posterior surface of the heart, lying anterior to the esophagus.
explanations.D: A laterally directed stab wound at the fifth intercostal space along the left midclavicular line enters the thorax lateral to the cardiac apex and penetrates the left lung (specifically the lingula of the superior lobe or inferior lobe). The left lung and pleura overlap the anterior chest wall in this region.
explanations.E: The right ventricle forms the vast majority of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart and lies directly behind the lower sternum (medial to the midclavicular line).

generalExplanation:
Thoracic cardiac and lung topography:
- Right ventricle: Forms the bulk of the anterior sternocostal surface; injured by parasternal penetrating wounds between the 3rd and 5th intercostal spaces.
- Left ventricle: Forms the cardiac apex, located at the left 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line.
- Left lung: Envelops and extends lateral to the cardiac apex; a laterally directed stab wound at the left 5th ICS in the MCL penetrates the anterior chest wall away from the heart, lacerating the left lung.
educationalObjective: The left ventricle forms the apex of the heart and can reach as far as the fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line (MCL). All other chambers of the heart lie medial to the left MCL. The lungs overlap much of the anterior surface of the heart.

stem: A 42-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to acute-onset shortness of breath. He has no medical conditions and does not use alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drugs. The patient works as a box handler at a warehouse and has excellent exercise tolerance. Family history is insignificant. Blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg and pulse is 112/min and regular. A short systolic murmur is heard at the apex. Bilateral crackles are present on lung auscultation. Bedside echocardiography reveals a flail posterior mitral leaflet due to chordal rupture and severe mitral regurgitation. Which of the following best reflects this patient's left ventricular hemodynamics compared to the normal heart?

options.A: Afterload decrease, preload decrease, ejection fraction decrease
options.B: Afterload decrease, preload increase, ejection fraction increase
options.C: Afterload increase, preload decrease, ejection fraction decrease
options.D: Afterload increase, preload decrease, ejection fraction increase
options.E: Afterload increase, preload increase, ejection fraction increase

explanations.A: Preload increases and ejection fraction increases in acute MR.
explanations.B: In acute severe mitral regurgitation (eg, spontaneous chordae tendineae rupture), during systole blood regurgitates into the low-pressure left atrium through the incompetent mitral valve in addition to forward flow into the aorta. This provides a low-resistance retrograde ejection pathway, markedly decreasing total left ventricular afterload. Regurgitant volume returning from the left atrium into the LV in subsequent diastole increases left ventricular end-diastolic volume (increased preload). The combination of reduced afterload and increased preload causes an increased left ventricular ejection fraction (hyperdynamic emptying), although net forward stroke volume into the aorta is substantially decreased, producing hypotension and pulmonary edema.
explanations.C: Afterload decreases due to the low-resistance leak into the left atrium.
explanations.D: Preload is increased due to regurgitant volume returning to the LV.
explanations.E: Afterload is decreased, not increased, because the regurgitant jet provides a low-pressure escape route for LV ejection.

generalExplanation:
Hemodynamics of acute mitral regurgitation:
1. Preload: Increased, because the left ventricle must accommodate both normal pulmonary venous return and the large regurgitant volume that backed up into the left atrium during the preceding systole.
2. Afterload: Decreased, because the open, incompetent mitral valve acts as a low-impedance parallel conduit for ventricular ejection alongside the high-pressure aorta.
3. Ejection Fraction: Increased (typically >70%), because lower afterload and augmented preload maximize systolic fiber shortening; however, forward cardiac output into the aorta drops precipitously.
educationalObjective: Regurgitant flow into the left atrium in acute mitral regurgitation leads to increased left atrial pressure and increased left ventricular end-diastolic volume (preload). The low-resistance regurgitant pathway also decreases left ventricular afterload with a resulting increase in ejection fraction but overall decrease in forward stroke volume. Increased left atrial pressure and decreased cardiac output result in pulmonary edema and severe hypotension, respectively.

stem: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents, who are concerned about her loss of interest in playing sports at school. During a recent competition, she walked off the field in the middle of the game, complaining about the pain in her legs. The patient has no other medical conditions and takes no medications. Her vaccination schedule is up-to-date. Physical examination shows pulsatile vessels within the intercostal spaces and diminished femoral pulses relative to brachial pulses. This patient's symptoms are most likely associated with which of the following conditions?

explanations.A: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) is associated with tetralogy of Fallot and interrupted aortic arch, presenting neonatally with hypocalcemia and thymic aplasia.
explanations.B: Down syndrome is associated with endocardial cushion defects (ostium primum ASD, complete AV canal).
explanations.C: Friedreich ataxia is associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
explanations.D: Kartagener syndrome is associated with situs inversus due to dynein arm defects.
explanations.E: Marfan syndrome is associated with cystic medial necrosis of the aorta, aortic dissection, and mitral valve prolapse.
explanations.F: Tuberous sclerosis is associated with cardiac rhabdomyomas.
explanations.G: The physical examination findings (diminished/delayed femoral pulses relative to upper extremity pulses, lower extremity claudication during exertion, and prominent collateral intercostal arterial pulsations with rib notching) are classic for postductal coarctation of the aorta. Up to 10% of females with Turner syndrome (45,XO) have congenital coarctation of the aorta; bicuspid aortic valve is also exceptionally common (30%).

generalExplanation: Coarctation of the aorta involves regional narrowing of the aortic lumen, typically occurring juxtaductally (just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery). In older children and adolescents, post-stenotic lower extremity hypoperfusion causes exertional leg fatigue and claudication, while proximal hypertension causes upper-to-lower extremity blood pressure gradients and delayed femoral pulses. Extensive collateral pathways develop via the internal thoracic, anterior intercostal, and posterior intercostal arteries, producing palpable intercostal pulsations and inferior rib notching on chest radiography. Coarctation of the aorta is strongly associated with Turner syndrome (45,XO).
educationalObjective: Aortic coarctation in a child/young adult presents with lower-extremity claudication (eg, pain and cramping with exercise), blood pressure discrepancy between the upper and lower extremities, and delayed or diminished femoral pulses. Turner syndrome (45,XO) is associated with coarctation of the aorta in up to 10% of cases.
